findings.title: Sender/installer validation is skipped entirely when the local Integration record does not yet exist
findings.body: When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch() immediately returns pipeline.next_step() (line 482) without ever checking the authenticated GitHub user against the installer. The Integration row (and its metadata['sender']) is only created/updated via an asynchronous GitHub webhook delivered independently of the OAuth redirect that brings the user back to Sentry. If the webhook has not yet been processed when the browser redirect reaches this view (a realistic race given both happen concurrently after installation), the exact cross-account hijack this PR is meant to prevent (attaching someone else's GitHub installation_id to an attacker-controlled Sentry org) is not blocked, because there is no local record yet to compare against.

findings.title: Unsafe dict access can raise uncaught KeyError instead of producing the error page
findings.body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes the `sender` key always exists in `metadata`. However `build_integration()` only sets `metadata['sender']` conditionally (`if state.get('sender')`), so integrations created without that state value (e.g. legacy installs, or installs where the webhook hasn't populated sender yet) will have no `sender` key. Accessing it directly will raise an unhandled KeyError, producing a 500 error instead of the intended graceful 'Invalid installation request.' response.

findings.title: Non-constant-time comparison for pipeline signature/state
findings.body: The OAuth `state` parameter is compared to `pipeline.signature` using plain `!=` rather than a constant-time comparison (e.g. `hmac.compare_digest`). For a PR specifically hardening the installation flow against forged state/signature values, using a non-constant-time string comparison leaves a (minor) timing side channel that a stricter implementation would avoid.

findings.title: Overly broad exception handling hides real token-exchange failures
findings.body: The `try/except Exception: payload = {}` block around parsing the GitHub token response silently swallows any error (malformed body, encoding issues, library/network bugs), not just malformed/erroneous OAuth responses. This makes it impossible to distinguish a genuine attacker/error scenario from an unrelated bug in parsing, and it will always present the same generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, potentially masking a legitimate internal error.

findings.title: No error handling around get_user_info call
findings.body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called without any try/except. If the GitHub `/user` API call fails (network error, rate limiting, ApiError), this will raise an unhandled exception and surface as a 500 error rather than the controlled installation-failed page used elsewhere in this view for comparable failure modes.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 'installation not found' code path
findings.body: The test now sends `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature used elsewhere in these tests (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). Because of the new state-mismatch check added in OAuthLoginView, the request now fails before ever reaching GitHubInstallation/build_integration, so the test only verifies the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message from the state check, not the intended scenario where GitHub's installation-info API returns 404 and build_integration raises IntegrationError('The GitHub installation could not be found.'). The original code path (404 handling in build_integration) is now untested, and a regression there would not be caught.
